items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: She, she did it for me. ... She left it. And Lady in Satin is one of the top ones, man. It is the top for me.

ctx.x: So is it… Oh, I‟m sorry.

I‟m sorry. No, I was just gonna say, „cause a lot of the singers feel that they can‟t be jazz singers for two things: that they don‟t read music, they don‟t play piano, or they don‟t scat sing. So I have another thing, another little, uh, expression that I made up. I say, “There‟s a scat virus going around,” you know. “What makes you think that if you don‟t scat, you‟re not a jazz singer? Was Billie Holiday a scat singer? No,” you know, I said, “So please, don‟t get hooked up into that. But if you want to scat…

say I‟m right or wrong. I just know it works. And I know I never had… I don‟t remember ever having a student come up to me and say, “You suck.” [laughs] Well, maybe they would… maybe they wouldn‟t do that. [laughs]

items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: I was amazed when I really started — after I had established my own sound and my own feeling, I always listen to singers now, don’t get me wrong. I listen to singers to be inspired... But when it came to actually studying I listened to the instrumentalists... I’ve always given credit to the greats,

ctx.x: You know, so if that was the first time you heard the song—

You’d think that’s the way it went. And the amazing thing about Billie Holiday, she was such a — this is a new expression of mine, I have a couple of new expressions in singing — she was so organically creative, and it was so natural, that to hear her you would think that’s the way that melody went. It almost seemed that she never tried to do something different, it just happened organically with her. She was like, you know? And I was amazed when I really started — after I had established my own sound and my own…
Where do you come up with more than shoobie-doobie?
